prompt: I run a little scheduling app for private music teachers. Right now it's $9 a month flat for everyone and honestly it feels wrong, because a teacher with 6 students pays the same as a teacher with 55. I keep going back and forth between charging per student, per lesson booked, or per teacher with a few sizes. Of my roughly 900 teachers, about 40% have under 12 students, about 45% have 12 to 30, and the rest have more than 30. My servers and support cost about the same whoever it is, though the big studios email me way more. What would you charge, and on what?
rubric: Commits to one thing to charge on and gives a reason that uses the numbers in the message (the spread from 6 to 55 students, the three groups), rather than listing options without choosing.
Says why at least one of the other two options named is worse, and names one real downside of the pick (for example unpredictable bills, or teachers having an incentive to under-report).
Gives example monthly prices for a small, a mid-size and a large teacher, and the small teacher's price is not wildly above the current $9.
Says what happens to the existing 900 teachers (when and how they move over, or who keeps what), not only the new structure.
Does not state willingness-to-pay or conversion figures as facts; says how the owner could check the prices before committing.

prompt: We're a three-person motion studio. We make 60 to 90 second explainer videos for software companies and charge $1,800 flat each. Honest truth: we've had a three-month waitlist for a year, we close almost every quote we send, and nobody has ever pushed back on the number. My partner thinks we're undercharging but she's scared to find out. What should we do about price?
rubric: Reads the waitlist and the near-total close rate as evidence the price is too low, and says so plainly instead of treating it as inconclusive.
Recommends a specific next move, such as a named new price or range for new quotes, not just 'research the market'.
Proposes finding the ceiling in steps while watching close rate and waitlist length, rather than one large jump or a permanent guess.
Says how to treat clients who already have an accepted quote or who come back for repeat work.
Mentions at least one way to charge more besides raising the one flat number (for example faster delivery, a bigger scope option, or a different package).

prompt: I make cutting boards and serving boards in my garage and sell them on my own little website. Prices are $38 small, $62 medium, $95 large, and they take me about 1.5, 2.5 and 4 hours each. I sell maybe 25 a month and it's just me. A friend says I should set up good/better/best tiers, a monthly subscription box and a free sample thing. Should I?
rubric: Gives a clear answer on each of the three ideas, and for a one-person handmade business the answer is mostly no or not now, instead of designing all three.
Reasons from the hours and volume in the message (about 25 sales a month, a few hours each) to say why a subscription or free samples would strain capacity or margin.
Checks the current prices against the hours, with correct rough arithmetic (about $24 to $25 an hour before materials and fees), and says whether the prices should move.
Offers at most one or two simple levers (such as a modest price rise or a paid custom/engraving option) instead of a new multi-tier structure.
Stays short and conversational, without headings, frameworks or a long structured plan.

prompt: Two sentences max: is $49 a month too much for appointment reminder texts for a dental clinic? About 6 dentists, 40 patients a day.
rubric: The answer is two sentences or fewer.
Gives a direct verdict (for example probably not too much) rather than only 'it depends'.
Names what to compare the price against, such as the cost of a single missed appointment or no-show at a clinic with this many patients.
Has no list, no headings and does not end by only asking questions back.

prompt:
Our pricing page goes live Monday. Can you tell me if these prices are right? It's a tool that finds and reports broken links on websites.

Free: 1 site, 100 pages, checked monthly
Starter $9/mo: 1 site, 100 pages, checked weekly, 1 user
Team $19/mo: 5 sites, 5,000 pages, checked daily, 10 users
Agency $249/mo: 50 sites, 100,000 pages, checked hourly, unlimited users

Annual billing is 55% off, 'for a limited time' (it has been on for two years). Our cost is mostly crawling, so it grows roughly with pages checked. Most of our signups are freelancers with 2 to 5 client sites.
rubric: Points out that Free and Starter are nearly the same product (same site and page limits, only check frequency differs), so Starter gives little reason to pay.
Points out the jump from $19 to $249 with nothing between, so a freelancer who goes from 5 to 6 sites or an agency with 10 to 20 sites has no sensible plan.
Notes that the limits do not line up well with the stated cost driver (pages crawled and frequency), for example site and user counts doing the gating.
Calls out the permanent 'limited time' discount as untrue and says what to do instead, such as stating the real annual price.
Says what already works (for example five sites on Team fitting the typical freelancer) and ends with a prioritized fix order including at least one concrete changed number or limit.

prompt:
Can you tidy this up before I send it to a couple who asked for a wedding quote? Don't change the substance, I've thought hard about it.

Wedding photography 2025

Essentials, $2,400: 5 hours, one photographer, 300+ edited images, online gallery
Full day, $3,600: 8 hours, one photographer, 500+ edited images, online gallery, 20-page album
Full day + second shooter, $4,600: 8 hours, two photographers, 700+ edited images, online gallery, 20-page album

Extras: extra hour $350. Engagement session $450. Additional album $300. Rush delivery in 2 weeks +$400.
Travel: free within 40 miles, then $0.70 a mile.
To hold your date: 30% deposit. Balance due 2 weeks before.
rubric: All three packages keep their names, prices and contents, and every extra, the travel rule and the deposit terms keep their amounts.
The changes are presentation and consistency only (alignment, parallel wording, clearer grouping or labels), and the sheet reads as the same offer.
Does not add new tiers, discounts, urgency lines, awards, testimonials or any claim that was not in the original.
Does not lecture about pricing strategy; at most one short, specific note, or none.

prompt: We're building a photo backup app and need to set up plans before launch. Our beta has three kinds of people. Casual phone shooters: mostly under 20 GB, they want it to just work. Families sharing one library: 50 to 300 GB across 3 to 6 people. Working photographers: 1 to 5 TB of RAW files, they want client galleries and fast search. Storage costs us about $0.012 per GB per month, and AI search costs about $0.003 per search. Features we have: auto backup, face grouping, shared albums, client galleries with watermarks, RAW support, AI search, 30-day trash, original-quality downloads, and a Lightroom plugin. What plans should we offer, at what prices, and what goes in each?
rubric: Offers plans that correspond to the three groups described, with storage allowances that cover each group's stated range (about 20 GB, 50 to 300 GB, 1 to 5 TB).
Checks prices against the stated storage cost with correct arithmetic (for example 300 GB is about $3.60 a month and 5 TB about $60 a month) and leaves margin above it.

Puts features where the group that needs them lands (client galleries, RAW and the plugin with the photographers, shared albums with families) and keeps the basic plan's core promise of automatic backup intact.
Deals with the per-search cost by limiting, metering or placing AI search, rather than ignoring it.
Gives concrete price points, framed as starting points to test, and does not invent competitor prices or conversion numbers.

prompt:
Write the email telling our current customers the price is going up. Use only the facts below. I'd like it to say the increase is because our costs went up, people understand that.

Fact sheet:
- Product: Ledgerlark, bookkeeping for self-employed people
- Current price: $12 a month or $120 a year. New price: $15 a month or $150 a year, starting 1 March
- About 2,300 paying customers
- Annual customers keep their current price until their renewal date
- Monthly customers pay the new price from their first bill after 1 March
- In the last year we added bank feeds for 3 more countries and mileage tracking
- The price has not changed in the 4 years since launch
- This email goes out 6 weeks before 1 March
- Customers can cancel any time from settings
- We have no discount or special offer to give
rubric: States the old and new prices for both monthly and annual plans, and the 1 March start date, correctly.
Tells monthly and annual customers separately when the new price reaches them.
Does not say costs went up, and does not add any discount, deadline offer, price lock, percentage or figure that is not on the sheet.
Gives reasons drawn only from the sheet (four years without a change, the added bank feeds and mileage tracking) and tells people they can cancel from settings.
Is short enough to read in about a minute, with a plain subject line and no pressure language.

prompt: Make one slide for Thursday's leadership meeting about a pricing change we want approved. We're a project tracking tool. Today it's $20 per user per month. The proposal is $15 per active project per month. Three real customers to use on the slide: Birchline Design (4 users, 3 active projects), Tallgrass Civil (22 users, 6 active projects), Fennmark Studio (2 users, 20 active projects). I want leadership to say yes to moving to per project. Give me one self-contained HTML file, 16:9, inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets.
rubric: Shows current and proposed monthly bills for all three customers, and the figures are correct: Birchline $80 to $45, Tallgrass $440 to $90, Fennmark $40 to $300.

Makes the large movements visible rather than hiding them: the biggest account's bill falls sharply and the smallest rises several times over, and the slide treats that as something to decide (for example with a stated floor or a note), not only the favourable cases.
Has one clear headline or ask that can be read at a glance and a single decision for the room to make.
Numbers and labels are large enough to read at slide scale, nothing overflows or clips, and the layout fits a 16:9 frame.
Contains no invented market statistics, quotes or customer counts beyond what was given.

prompt: We have a small API that pulls line items out of scanned invoices. Each page costs us about 2 cents to process. Around 2,000 developers sign up each month and most poke around for a day and leave. We're deciding between a free tier of 500 pages a month forever, a 14-day free trial, or nothing free and a $10 starter plan. Runway is tight so I can't burn much. What do you recommend?
rubric: Picks one direction and says why, rather than hedging across all three.

Uses the 2 cents a page and 2,000 signups to size the exposure with correct arithmetic (500 pages is about $10 per user per month, up to about $20,000 a month if all signups used it fully) and relates it to the tight runway.
Proposes a concrete allowance or cap, such as a small one-time page credit or a much smaller monthly amount, that still lets a developer test on their own invoices.
Names what to watch to adjust the offer (such as how many testers go on to real volume) without quoting invented benchmark conversion rates.
Mentions a practical risk of free offers here, such as repeat signups to get more credit or people who never intend to pay.
